questions.prompt: In Git, what is the purpose of the 'staging area' (or index) before committing changes?

options.text: It automatically uploads your local changes to a remote repository like GitHub.
It acts as a preparation area where you can select exactly which changes to include in your next commit.
It permanently deletes untracked files to clean up your working directory.
It merges conflicting branches automatically before saving your work.

questions.explanation: The staging area allows developers to review and format their commits by choosing specific files or modifications to include, separating the working directory state from the actual repository history.

questions.prompt: Which of the following best describes the relationship between Git and GitHub?

options.text: Git is the programming language used to write GitHub's web interface.
Git is a local command-line tool for version control, while GitHub is a cloud-based hosting service for Git repositories.
Git is only used for small personal projects, whereas GitHub is required for large enterprise software.
Git and GitHub are identical tools developed by the same team, with GitHub being the newer name.

questions.explanation: Git is the underlying open-source version control system that runs locally on your machine, while GitHub is a web-based platform that hosts Git repositories and provides collaboration features.

questions.prompt: What is the primary difference between running 'git fetch' and 'git pull'?

options.text: 'git fetch' downloads remote changes without merging them, while 'git pull' downloads and immediately merges them.
'git fetch' only works on private repositories, while 'git pull' works on public ones.
'git fetch' uploads local commits, while 'git pull' downloads remote commits.
'git fetch' creates a new branch, while 'git pull' deletes an existing branch.

questions.explanation: 'git fetch' safely retrieves updates from the remote repository without changing your local working files, whereas 'git pull' is a shortcut that performs a fetch and then automatically merges those updates into your current branch.

questions.prompt: You are trying to merge a feature branch into the main branch, and Git reports a merge conflict. What is the correct way to handle this?

options.text: Git will automatically choose the newest changes and discard the older ones, so you don't need to do anything.
You must delete the feature branch and recreate your changes manually on the main branch.
Open the conflicted files, manually choose which changes to keep, remove the conflict markers, stage the files, and commit the resolution.
Run 'git push --force' to overwrite the conflicting changes on the remote server.

questions.explanation: Merge conflicts happen when Git cannot automatically reconcile differences; developers must manually edit the files to resolve the conflicts, stage the corrected files, and make a new commit.

questions.prompt: You have pushed a commit to a shared remote repository, but realize it contains a bug. What is the safest way to undo this change without disrupting your team members' histories?

options.text: Use 'git reset --hard' to delete the commit locally, then force-push to the remote repository.
Use 'git revert' to create a new commit that records the exact opposite of the buggy commit's changes.
Delete the repository on GitHub and recreate it from your local backup.
Manually delete the files affected by the bug and make a standard new commit.

questions.explanation: 'git revert' is safe for shared repositories because it creates a new commit that undoes the changes, preserving the commit history and preventing synchronization issues for other developers.

questions.prompt: When you check out a specific commit hash directly (detached HEAD state) instead of a branch name, what happens if you make new commits?

options.text: The commits are saved to the main branch automatically.
Git prevents you from making any commits until you switch back to an active branch.
The commits are made but are not associated with any branch, meaning they can easily be lost if you switch branches without creating a new branch reference.
The commits overwrite the history of the commit you checked out, permanently altering the past.

questions.explanation: In a detached HEAD state, you are not on any branch. Commits made here are orphaned and will eventually be cleaned up by Git's garbage collection unless you create a branch to point to them.
